units.name: Words and Their Jobs
units.summary: The different jobs words do in a sentence.

units.name: Building Sentences
units.summary: Putting words together so they make complete sense.

topics.name: Nouns and Verbs
topics.summary: Naming words and doing words, and how to spot each one.

topics.name: Complete Sentences
topics.summary: What every sentence needs before it is finished.

objectives.text: Find the nouns in a sentence.
Find the verb in a sentence.
Use a test to check whether a word is a noun or a verb.

keyTerms.definition: A word that names a person, place, animal or thing.
A word that tells what someone or something does.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Every word in a sentence has a job. Two of the most important jobs are naming and doing. Once you can spot those two, sentences make much more sense.

sections.heading: Nouns name things
sections.body:
A NOUN names something. It can be:

    a person — teacher, mother, Musu
    a place  — market, school, river
    an animal — goat, fish, bird
    a thing  — book, rice, chair

A quick test: can you put "a", "an" or "the" in front of it and does it still sound right?

    the book ✓ — so "book" is a noun
    the jump ✗ — "jump" is not usually a noun

sections.heading: Verbs tell what happens
sections.body:
A VERB tells what someone or something does.

    run, eat, write, sleep, carry, laugh

In this sentence:

    The boy carries water.

    "boy"   — names a person → noun
    "water" — names a thing  → noun
    "carries" — tells what he does → verb

A quick test: can you put "I" or "she" in front of it?

    she carries ✓ — so "carries" is a verb
    she book ✗   — so "book" is not a verb
sections.example:
Finding both in one sentence.

    The farmer plants cassava.

Ask two questions, in order:

Who or what is this about?
    The farmer. That names a person → NOUN

What does the farmer do?
    Plants. That is the action → VERB

Is anything else named?
    Cassava. That names a thing → NOUN

So: farmer (noun), plants (verb), cassava (noun).

sections.heading: One word, two jobs
sections.body:
Careful — some words can do either job. Look at what the word is DOING in that sentence, not just the word by itself.

    I drink water.        Here "drink" is a verb. It tells the action.
    Bring me a drink.     Here "drink" is a noun. It names a thing.

Same word. Different job. This is why you test the word inside its sentence.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Find the nouns and the verb in each sentence:

1. The goat eats grass.
2. My sister sweeps the yard.
3. Children play football.

Then: write your own sentence with two nouns and one verb.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A noun names a person, place, animal or thing.
• A verb tells what someone or something does.
• Noun test: does "the" fit in front of it?
• Verb test: does "she" fit in front of it?
• Some words can be either — check the job it does in THAT sentence.

objectives.text: Say the two things every sentence must have.
Tell a complete sentence from an incomplete one.
Use a capital letter and a full stop correctly.

keyTerms.definition: A group of words that makes complete sense on its own.
Who or what the sentence is about.
The dot (.) that shows a sentence has ended.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Some groups of words are finished. Others leave you waiting for more. This lesson shows you how to tell the difference, and how to fix the unfinished ones.

sections.heading: Two things every sentence needs
sections.body:
A complete sentence needs:

    1. A SUBJECT — who or what it is about
    2. A VERB — what they do

Look:

    The dog barks.

    Subject: the dog
    Verb: barks

It is finished. You are not left waiting.

Now look at this:

    The dog in the yard.

Who is it about? The dog. Good.
What does the dog do? …nothing is said.

You are left waiting. It is not a sentence yet.

sections.heading: The waiting test
sections.body:
Read the words out loud. When you stop, do you feel finished, or do you feel like something is missing?

    Running to the market.        → Who is running? MISSING
    Musu is running to the market. → Finished ✓

    Because it rained.            → Because it rained, what? MISSING
    We stayed inside because it rained. → Finished ✓

That feeling of waiting is real information. Trust it.
sections.example:
Fixing three incomplete groups.

1. "The tall boy."
   Has a subject, no verb. Add one:
   → The tall boy waved.

2. "Sings every morning."
   Has a verb, no subject. Add one:
   → My mother sings every morning.

3. "After we ate."
   Leaves you waiting. Finish the thought:
   → After we ate, we washed the plates.

Each fix adds the missing part. Nothing else changed.

sections.heading: Capital letter and full stop
sections.body:
Every sentence starts with a CAPITAL letter and ends with a FULL STOP.

    wrong:  the rain stopped
    right:  The rain stopped.

Think of them as a door. The capital opens the sentence, the full stop closes it. Without them the reader cannot tell where one idea ends and the next begins.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Which of these are complete sentences? Fix the ones that are not:

1. The market is busy.
2. Walking down the road.
3. My brother.
4. We carried the water home.
5. When the sun set.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Every sentence needs a subject and a verb.
• Read it aloud: if you feel like you are waiting, it is not finished.
• Missing subject → add who or what.
• Missing verb → add what they do.
• Start with a capital letter, end with a full stop.

questions.question: In the sentence "The goat eats grass", which word is the verb?
questions.explanation: "Eats" tells you what the goat does, so it is the verb. "Goat" and "grass" are both nouns — they name an animal and a thing. Try the test: "she eats" sounds right, but "she goat" does not.

questions.question: How many nouns are in "My sister sweeps the yard"?
questions.explanation: Two: "sister" names a person and "yard" names a place. "Sweeps" is the verb, and "my" and "the" are neither. Check each word with the test — "the sister" and "the yard" both sound right, but "the sweeps" does not.

questions.question: In "Bring me a drink", what job does the word "drink" do?
questions.explanation: Here "drink" names a thing you can bring, so it is a noun — notice "a drink" sounds right. In "I drink water" the same word is a verb, because there it tells the action. Always check the job the word does in that particular sentence.

questions.question: Which of these is a complete sentence?
questions.explanation: "The market is busy" has a subject (the market) and a verb (is), and nothing is left hanging. The others leave you waiting: walking — who? my brother — did what? when the sun set — then what happened?

questions.question: What is missing from "Sings every morning"?
questions.explanation: It has a verb — "sings" — but never says WHO sings, so the subject is missing. Add one and it is finished: "My mother sings every morning." Ask "who or what?" and if there is no answer, the subject is what is missing.
